An image as a function, drawn

Every network so far took an image in. Here the network is the image. You train a small MLP so that feeding it a pixel's coordinates returns that pixel's value: f(x, y) → value. Add time and it becomes a video: f(x, y, t) → value. Because it is a function and not a grid, you can ask it about a time that was never filmed, which is 5f. The whole question is six steps of one idea, and almost every bug is a shape bug, so each section lists the shapes.

5a · MLP, sample_image, predict_imageFit one frame from raw (x, y): sections 1 and 2.
5b · positional_embedding_power_ls, MLP_PEWhy raw coordinates give a blur and sines fix it: section 3.
5c, 5d · sample_images, time encodingAdd t, then encode it or not: sections 4 and 5.
5e, 5f · partition_index, 100 framesBatches of at most 16,000, and what interpolation reveals: sections 6 and 7.

1 · the idea

An image is a table of (where, what) rows

Your notes list an image as a signal x[x, y] on a pixel grid and a video as x[x, y, t] W4 Table 1. Read that as a function: put in a position, get out a value. A grid stores the answers. An implicit representation stores a rule that computes them W4 Table 2. To learn the rule, turn the image into a supervised dataset: one row per pixel, input = its coordinates, label = its value. Move over the picture to see rows.

Frame 4 of my stand-in animation: 128 × 128 pixels, each 0 (background) or 1 (figure). 16,384 rows in all.

WHAT sample_image(image, 8) RETURNS
sampled_positionsfloat32, shape (n, 2). With scaled=True each coordinate is divided by the image's size along that axis, so it lies in [0, 1). pixel_valuesshape (n,). The value at each sampled position, in the same order.
Three things that decide whether 5a works at all. (1) One convention for the two coordinates. An image tensor is indexed [row, column]. Whichever order you put the two numbers in when sampling, predict_image must build its grid in the same order and reshape back the same way, or the prediction comes out transposed. (2) Scale. Raw indices 0…127 are large inputs for a network; dividing by the size puts them in [0, 1), and the encoding in 5b assumes that range. (3) The label's type. The docstring returns integer pixel values; a loss needs floats, and the network's output has shape (n, 1) while the labels are (n,). Make the two shapes equal before subtracting, or broadcasting silently builds an n × n matrix.

2 · question 5a · the MLP

Two numbers in, one number out, a stack of affine maps and ReLUs between

The model is the MLP from your notes: h(0) = x, h(ℓ) = φ(Wℓ h(ℓ−1) + bℓ) W3 §3.1.1 W2 §2.5. The four constructor arguments in your cell map onto it directly. Without the nonlinearity φ the whole stack collapses to one affine map W2 §2.5, which for (x, y) is a tilted plane: a brightness ramp.

input_dimension2
nb_layers4
embedding_dimension128

I count nb_layers as the number of hidden Linear + ReLU blocks, followed by one output Linear. Your brief does not define it more precisely, so state your own reading in a comment. The last layer has no ReLU. Since the target is 0 or 1 and the plotting cell thresholds at 0.5, a sigmoid on the output is natural W2 §2.5: “apply sigmoid for binary output”. Either squared error or binary cross-entropy against the 0/1 label then works; my demo uses cross-entropy.

The training loop, and what it does to the picture

each step positions, values = sample_image(image, n) a random mini-batch of pixels W2 §3.4
prediction = model(positions) shape (n, 1)
loss = mean( (prediction − values)² ) or cross-entropy shapes made equal first
zero the gradients, loss.backward(), optimizer.step()
sometimes accuracy = mean( (predict_image(image) > 0.5) == image ) over all H·W pixels
append (epoch, loss) and (epoch, accuracy) to the two lists the plotting cell reads x[0], x[1]

predict_image, in shapes. Build every coordinate of the image once: H·W rows of 2 numbers, in the same order and scaling as the sampler. Run the model on them without tracking gradients, reshape the (H·W, 1) output to (H, W), and return it on the CPU as the docstring says. If the picture comes out transposed or sheared, the order of your grid and your reshape disagree.

3 · question 5b · positional encoding

Give the network sines and cosines of the position, not the position

Two neighbouring pixels differ by 1/128 in x. To turn that tiny difference into a jump from 0 to 1, a network fed raw coordinates needs enormous weights, and gradient descent finds smooth functions long before it finds sharp ones. So change the features, the move your notes call φ(x) W1 §1.2 and the one Q1 made with polynomial terms. Each coordinate p becomes cos(2l·π·p) and sin(2l·π·p) for l = 0 … L−1: waves that double in frequency each time. It is the same sinusoid idea your notes give for transformers W3 §3.8.2, with powers of two.

L (frequencies)7
position p0.500

The encoded vector for this position: L cosines (blue) then L sines (green), each between −1 and 1. Drag p by one pixel and watch the right-hand bars of each colour flip while the left-hand ones barely move.

X (n, d) d = 2 for (x, y), 3 for (x, y, t)
freqs = cst · 2^[0 … L−1] (L,) cst = π by default
X[..., None] · freqs (n, d, L) every coordinate times every frequency
flatten the last two axes (n, d·L)
cos(…), sin(…) (n, d·L) each
cat([cos, sin], axis=−1) (n, 2·d·L) the template's return line fixes this order: all cosines, then all sines

MLP_PE is a thin wrapper: encode, then call the MLP from 5a. So the inner MLP's input_dimension is 2·L·input_dimension, not input_dimension, and its other three arguments pass straight through. Decide what positional_enc_L = 0 means (no encoding, inner input size unchanged) and handle it, because the default argument is 0.

4 · question 5c · adding time

One more input column, eleven times the rows

Nothing about the network changes except its input size. The dataset changes: a row is now (x, y, t) → value, and there are N_frames · H · W of them. Your notes: “for video, represent both space and time” W3 §3.8.2. Pick a frame and move over it.

images(N_frames, H, W) = (11, 128, 128) in your notebook. sample_images → positions(n, 3): two spatial coordinates and the frame's time, each scaled by its own axis length when scaled=True. sample_images → values(n,): images[frame, row, column] for each sampled triple. predict_imagesbuild all N_frames·H·W rows, predict, reshape to (N_frames, H, W). 11·128·128 = 180,224 rows. eval_mean_accuracythresholded prediction equal to the truth, averaged over every pixel of every frame.
Two details that come back in 5f. (1) Which number is t? “Divide by the dimension” gives frame k the time k / N_frames, so the frames sit at 0, 1/11, …, 10/11 and the last frame is not at t = 1. Dividing by N_frames − 1 instead puts them at 0, 0.1, …, 1 (my demo does this). Either is fine if you use the same rule everywhere; “between the first and last frame” in 5f means between the times your training actually used. (2) Column order. The model only sees a matrix. If the sampler writes (x, y, t) and the predictor writes (t, x, y), nothing crashes and the output is noise.

5 · question 5d · encode time, or not

Same network, two ways of feeding it t

With encode_time_dimension=True all three columns are encoded. With False, only x and y are, and t is appended as the raw number. That changes the input size, which is the one thing to get right in MLP_PE_time_option.

encode time = True cos and sin of (x, y, t) at L frequencies inner input size = 2·L·3 = 42 for L = 7
encode time = False cos and sin of (x, y), then raw t appended inner input size = 2·L·2 + 1 = 29 for L = 7
training frame

The nested lists in your training cell are loss_list[0] / accuracy_list[0] for time encoding ON and [1] for OFF, each a list of (epoch, value) pairs, and the two trained models go into the two variables the save cell names. The third column on this page (time encoded with only 2 frequencies) is an extra of mine; your function's signature has one L for everything.

6 · question 5e · batching

Cut the rows into chunks of at most 16,000

Predicting 100 frames means 1,638,400 rows. Pushing them through at once makes every hidden layer hold a 1,638,400 × width matrix. Instead, slice the row list into consecutive ranges [i, j), run each on its own, and join the outputs in order. partition_index(totalsize, chunksize) only produces the list of (i, j) pairs.

totalsize
chunksize
presets
The cases a marker will try. A total that is an exact multiple of the chunk (no empty last pair). A total smaller than one chunk (exactly one pair, (0, total)). The last pair ending at exactly totalsize, never beyond. Your notes make the same point about training batches: “the final smaller batch should use its actual size” W2 §3.4. The docstring says “equal chunk”, and the question says the size must not exceed 16,000: every chunk but possibly the last is full, and none is larger.

In predict_images: build the full coordinate matrix on the CPU, loop over the pairs, move only rows [i, j) to the device, predict inside torch.no_grad(), move each result back to the CPU, concatenate in order, reshape to (N_frames, H, W). Without no_grad PyTorch also stores every activation for a backward pass that never comes, and the batching saves much less.

7 · question 5f · 100 frames from 11

Ask the function about moments that were never filmed

Take 100 times evenly spaced from the first training time to the last, build the (x, y, t) rows for each, predict in batches, threshold, write the frames. 89 of the 100 lie between training frames, where no loss ever told the network what to do. Because I drew this animation from a formula, I also have the true in-between frames, so the page can score each network at every one of the 100 times. You will not have that for the horse; you judge by watching.

Click a picture above to choose a row. Each strip below stacks that one row of pixels for all 100 times, so across = x, down = t. Continuous motion draws smooth slanted bands. Motion that only exists at the training frames draws a staircase or broken bands.

What your notes say about this. “High accuracy at observed frames does not guarantee smooth or meaningful interpolation.” W3 §3.11.3 And on sinusoidal positions: “Encoding a position is not a guarantee of reliable extrapolation” W3 §3.8.2. Training accuracy (section 5) and the curve above are different questions. The brief's own wording, “if you overfit on the training frames, it would give a discontinuous or jagged motion”, is a statement about the second.
  1. Times. 100 values from your first training time to your last, with the same scaling as training (section 4).
  2. Rows. For each time, all H·W positions with that t in the time column: 100·H·W rows, predicted through your batching.
  3. Frames. Reshape to (100, H, W), threshold at 0.5, convert to uint8 0/255 as the notebook's own video cell does, and write them to the given output path.
  4. Which model? You have two from 5d. Watch both videos before choosing which one to submit, and say why.
